slides.title: Brand Strategy & Positioning
slides.subtitle: The brand is not what you build. It is what you consistently decline to build.

slides.title: Ask what Stripe *declines* to do
slides.lead: Read their site, their docs, Collison's writing, the API changelog. Then ask: what is Stripe's brand?
bullets: Most people answer by listing output — clean APIs, developer-first infrastructure, docs that ship as a product. All real. All the wrong answer.
What makes a brand legible across a dozen product lines is not what a company consistently *produces*. It is what it consistently **declines** to produce.

Pile the refusals on top of each other and you get a company that looks as if it always knew what it was — precisely because it kept declining the things that would have made it look like something else.

slides.title: Marketing is downstream of brand
slides.lead: Two different questions, and only one of them comes first.
bullets: **Marketing strategy** answers: *how do we reach our audience?* Channels, messages, funnels, ad spend.
**Brand strategy** answers: *who are we, for whom, and what will we never compromise?*
Without the constraint set, marketing decisions get made in isolation — the ad targets everyone, the message says nothing, the product ships a feature for every customer who asks.
The company loses shape as it grows.

slides.title: Mission, Vision, Values, UVP
slides.lead: Seven components, each doing a job the other six cannot.
bullets: **Mission** — one sentence, specific and testable. *Increase the GDP of the internet* is testable. *Make payments easier* is not: easier than what, for whom, by how much?

**Vision** — the world if you succeed. Every business anywhere transacting online with the reliability and cost structure of a Fortune 500 company. Ambitious enough to motivate, specific enough to steer.
**Values** — the commitments you maintain *when maintaining them is costly*. A value that has never cost you anything is a preference waiting to be overridden by the first deadline.
**UVP** — one sentence a customer could falsify. Stripe's at launch: the cleanest payment API available, integrable in seven lines of code, with documentation that did not require a sales call.

slides.title: Archetype, Voice, Positioning
slides.lead: The three that decide how the whole thing sounds and where it stands.
bullets: **Archetype** — the strategic anchor. It does not determine what you decide; it determines that your decisions **cohere**.
**Voice** — sentence rhythm, vocabulary, formats favored and rejected. Not aesthetic preference: voice encodes audience and archetype simultaneously.

**Positioning** — where you sit relative to the *actual* alternative the customer considers. For Stripe in 2010 that was not PayPal. It was writing your own payment integration, or not building the feature at all.
Positioning against the actual alternative produces a completely different strategy than positioning against a named competitor.

slides.title: Every adjacent pair has to answer to the next
slides.lead: Each component constrains the others. When they contradict, the brand is incoherent — and incoherent brands do not scale.
slides.why: chapter: "Before you finalize, run the coherence check on every adjacent component pair" — and names the pairs (Mission/UVP, Values/negative space, Archetype/voice, Positioning/UVP); fig-07 draws the seven components in a ring with the consistency question on each edge

slides.title: You decide before the pressure, or the pressure decides
slides.lead: Every startup makes brand decisions. Most make them reactively — and reactive decisions compound.
slides.why: chapter: "The companies that navigate those moments well made the decisions *in advance*, when the reasoning was clear and the pressure was low" — and names the moments; "Someone reading your strategy in two years should be able to check whether you kept your commitments"

commit.label: the one page, signed while pressure is low

data.axisLabel: the strategy is written before the evidence arrives

slides.title: The pattern of refusals *is* the brand
slides.lead: Run the inversion on Stripe. Both columns are load-bearing — but only one of them is the part you can recognize.
slides.why: chapter runs an explicit sorting: "Run the inversion test on Stripe. They declined enterprise sales processes... declined the broad small-business market... declined to compete with PayPal on consumer trust... declined rapid product proliferation... declined marketing-style content." fig-04 is literally built vs declined

data.note: The chapter counts neither column. Any single refusal could be a one-time choice; the sustained pattern is the brand.

slides.title: Four criteria, and most no-lists fail the first two
slides.lead: At least five entries. Each item has to survive all four tests — the chapter's own examples pass and fail in public.
slides.why: chapter names four criteria (Specific · Archetype-consistent · Costly · Testable over time) and applies them to named example items: the settings-panel item passes Specific, "features that compromise simplicity" is decorative, enterprise SSO against a six-figure contract is costly, "a feature nobody asked for" is not

slides.title: Not your archetype. The one your audience needs.
slides.lead: In earlier chapters you named a personal archetype. Here the question changes shape.
bullets: The question is not *what is my personal archetype?* It is: **what archetype does this product's audience need the company to be?**
A developer integrating payments needs a **Sage** — a company that knows the domain better than they do and shares it without condescension or sales pressure.
A first-time founder in a hostile regulatory environment needs a **Caregiver**. A challenger against an entrenched incumbent may need a **Rebel**.
Four questions to the audience: what do they *fear*, *want to achieve*, *distrust*, and *reward*? The reward structure points at the archetype.

slides.title: Name the failure mode your strength produces
slides.lead: Every archetype has a shadow — the failure mode produced by taking its strength too far.
bullets: The Sage's shadow is **dogmatism**: so committed to depth and rigor that the company goes rigid, iterates too slowly, or dismisses evidence that contradicts its model.
Stripe's API versioning policy — maintaining every version indefinitely rather than deprecating — is a rigor that is also a burden. **The shadow is the cost of the strength.**
Name your shadow in the document as a failure mode to *monitor*, not one you are already living in.

A Rebel founder can run a Caregiver company. The reverse — a Caregiver founder running a Rebel brand — is more common, and the brand drifts toward the founder's comfort rather than the audience's need.

slides.title: Three tests, then the one the frameworks omit
slides.lead: A startup name is a load-bearing architectural decision. Changing it after market presence is expensive and disorienting.
slides.why: chapter: "Three tests, applied before you commit" — the bar test, the lawyer test, the domain test — "Then add a fourth test that standard frameworks omit: archetype alignment... Eliminate candidates that fail archetype alignment regardless of their trademark status or domain availability." Every verdict depends on the reader's own name

gates.label: The bar test
gates.rule: said once, in noise — spelled and recalled thirty seconds later

gates.label: The lawyer test
gates.rule: USPTO TESS, close phonetic variants, Class 42

gates.label: The domain test
gates.rule: .com available or acquirable at a price you can pay

gates.label: Archetype alignment
gates.rule: eliminates regardless of the other three

slides.title: A name that fights its archetype is fighting itself
slides.lead: *Stripe* fits the Sage: simple, precise, no emotional charge, no promise beyond what the product delivers. *BlazingFast* would start from a brand deficit with the audience it wants.
slides.why: chapter enumerates naming tendencies by archetype with named examples: "Sage names... Stripe, Linear, Notion, Vercel, Supabase... Hero names... Salesforce, Crowdstrike, Cloudflare. Caregiver names... Calm, Headspace. Magician names... Palantir, Anthropic, OpenAI" — a two-level taxonomy; fig-08 spans six archetypes, two of which the chapter gives no examples for

slides.title: One page is a specification test, not a formatting preference
slides.lead: A brand strategy that runs to two pages has not been finished. It is still listing options rather than committing to positions.
slides.why: chapter: "A brand strategy document that runs to two pages has not been finished... Every section must be compressed to its essential commitment, stripped of the explanatory prose that makes vagueness comfortable" — an explicit boundary with named things that must not cross it

slides.title: Two identical products. One keeps a no-list.
slides.lead: A brand becomes legible when an audience can predict what a company will and will not do. Predictability is built by consistency. Consistency requires constraint.
slides.why: chapter's closing thought experiment is a literal divergence: "Suppose two companies ship identical products in the same quarter. Company A has an explicit no-list maintained consistently. Company B has no no-list... A's customers know what they are buying. B's customers are confused... A's team knows what to build. B's team spends [time] in prioritization debates the no-list would have resolved"

slides.section: what this deck will not tell you
slides.title: Every grey slot is a decision you still owe
slides.lead: Nothing on the preceding slides was filled in from a guess, and the chapter's own honesty note applies here too.
bullets: Whether your name clears the bar, the lawyer, the domain, and the archetype — **TO RUN**. Whether your no-list items are costly and testable — **TO RUN**.
Stripe's success is over-determined. Payments in 2010 was structurally favorable to a developer-first entrant; brand discipline is not a complete causal explanation.
The defensible claim is narrower: brand discipline did not hurt, the mechanisms are internally coherent, and the compounding advantage of maintained coherence is visible in the case we can study.
The still-open question: at what stage does a strategy stop being a useful constraint and start preventing necessary adaptation?

slides.title: Write the page. Then write the list of nos you will be held to.
slides.lead: Five items, each specific, archetype-consistent, costly, and checkable in two years. Show the list — and only the list — to someone who has not read your strategy, and ask them to name your archetype. If they guess right, it is working.
